title: Ansel and the Safehouse
premise: Paloma Pemberton, a whistle-blower living under four names in the border town of Ansel, has spent seven years following the safehouse's shifting rules. When every record of Flight 447 vanishes while the plane is still airborne — and it lands carrying a passenger who shouldn't exist — Paloma realizes the network that once protected him is now erasing people, including his old handler. To survive the night before the border checkpoint shifts change, he must trade the one secret worth killing for: proof of who inside the safehouse is rewriting reality itself. In the end, Paloma chooses truth over loyalty, exposing the archivist behind the disappearances at the cost of his own records — and walks across the border as no one at all.
about_author: Ines Villalobos is the pen name of a former border-region journalist who spent a decade covering displacement and document fraud before turning to fiction. She writes thrillers about ordinary people trapped inside systems that quietly rewrite them.

chapters.title: Four Names
chapters.summary: Paloma Pemberton's POV. A routine morning in Ansel: he recites his four identities over coffee, checks the safehouse bulletin for rewritten rules, and notes that rule seven has changed again overnight. The beat is quiet dread — a man whose life depends on paperwork he no longer controls.

chapters.title: The Bulletin
chapters.summary: Paloma visits the safehouse drop to collect new documents and finds the clerk, Marisol, visibly frightened; someone has already queried his file twice this week. POV stays with Paloma. Emotional beat: the first crack in his belief that the system protects its own.

chapters.title: Flight 447
chapters.summary: At the internet café, Paloma watches flight-tracking data for 447 simply vanish mid-air while the plane is still broadcasting. Other patrons saw nothing wrong. His POV. Beat: vertigo — the world's records can be edited in real time, and only he noticed.

chapters.title: The Passenger Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Paloma meets the plane at the small terminal out of habit. Among deplaning passengers is Elias Voss, his former handler, officially dead for three years. Voss slips him a matchbook. Paloma's POV; beat: terror braided with hope that an ally survives.

chapters.title: Rule Seven
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She explains what she knows: the safehouse has begun 'archiving' people — deleting their records so thoroughly they never existed. Rule seven now forbids acknowledging archived persons. Beat: complicity and guilt as she breaks her own rule by warning him.

chapters.title: Matchbook
chapters.summary: Paloma decodes the matchbook: coordinates to a derelict cannery and a time — 11 p.m., one hour before the checkpoint shifts change. En route he spots a gray sedan tailing him. His POV; beat: the hunted animal waking up, adrenaline sharpening memory.

chapters.title: Voss, Alive Enough
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. In the cannery he confesses he let himself be archived to hide inside the deletion — the only place the network doesn't look. He reveals the secret worth killing for: a ledger naming who commands the rewrites. Beat: bitter reunion, trust frayed by seven years of lies.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Paloma reads the ledger fragment: deletions authorized under a signature code belonging to someone inside Ansel's own safehouse. His POV. Beat: betrayal — the sanctuary was always the predator, and loyalty has been the trap all along.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She calculates the shift change: between 11:40 and midnight, the checkpoint runs on skeleton staff with unverified rosters — the only window to move a person or a secret across. Beat: cold competence masking fear for Paloma.

chapters.title: The Gray Sedan
chapters.summary: Paloma is ambushed near the fish market; he escapes through the cannery's freezing tunnels but loses the ledger copy. His POV. Beat: panic giving way to grim resourcefulness — he memorizes the names instead, making himself the archive.

chapters.title: Interrogation of a Ghost
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Captured briefly by the network's 'reconciliation team,' Voss stalls them with bureaucratic jargon and escapes when Marisol triggers a false archive alert. Beat: dark comedy curdling into horror at how easily procedure becomes violence.

chapters.title: Memory as Evidence
chapters.summary: Paloma, hiding in a chapel loft, writes the ledger names from memory onto his own skin in ink. His POV, interleaved with flashbacks to the original whistle-blowing that started everything. Beat: the body becoming the last honest record.

chapters.title: Marisol's Choice
chapters.summary: Marisol is confronted by Deputy Director Hale — the safehouse's beloved father figure — who offers her promotion for Paloma's location. Her POV. Beat: temptation and disgust; she lies to Hale's face and crosses her own point of no return.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Paloma infiltrates the safehouse basement and finds the deletion machine: racks of drives and a printing press producing retroactive history. He photographs everything. His POV. Beat: awe and nausea — power revealed not as force but as editing.

chapters.title: Hale's Offer
chapters.summary: Hale catches Paloma in the archive and, surprisingly, talks: offers him a clean identity abroad if he surrenders the ledger. Paloma's POV. Beat: the seduction of safety — the same bargain he made seven years ago, recognized too late.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss sacrifices himself creating a diversion at the depot, buying Paloma the hour he needs, and is re-archived — erased mid-sentence on a phone call. Beat: grief and fury; loyalty vindicated only in its spending.

chapters.title: Eleven Forty
chapters.summary: Marisol falsifies the shift roster and meets Paloma at the checkpoint fence with a forged manifest listing him as cargo. Their POV alternates. Beat: taut, procedural suspense — every second accounted for, trust finally earned.

chapters.title: The Trade
chapters.summary: At the checkpoint, Hale arrives personally. Paloma makes the trade he promised the blurb: he hands over a decoy ledger while broadcasting the real names to every press outlet and foreign consulate via the café's open line. His POV. Beat: climax — truth released cannot be deleted.

chapters.title: Midnight Roster
chapters.summary: The shift changes; the new guards have no orders matching Hale's. Marisol walks Paloma through as 'verified freight.' Hale is detained by his own reconciliation team, archived by the machine he wielded. Alternating POV. Beat: ironic justice, breath held then released.

chapters.title: Afterimages
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, days later. The safehouse is under external audit; deletions are being reversed piecemeal, some people returning to families who half-remember them. She keeps rule seven torn from the wall. Beat: mourning mixed with fragile repair.

chapters.title: No One At All
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Across the border with no documents, no name, no file anywhere — free precisely because he erased himself. He begins writing the true account longhand, on paper, in his own hand. Beat: bittersweet liberation; memory as the only citizenship left.

chapters.title: Ansel, Still Standing
chapters.summary: Final chapter, omniscient-close on the town. Ansel functions as always; the bulletin board posts new rules; travelers pass the checkpoint without knowing what nearly happened there. Last image: a matchbook on the café counter, unopened. Beat: quiet resonance — systems persist, but so do witnesses.
